- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
I'll write about the particular loneliness of being awake when everyone else is asleep.

There's something about 3 AM that feels like a secret. The world has stopped pretending. No one is performing productivity or cheerfulness or any of the small social contracts we maintain during daylight hours. The house settles. The refrigerator hums its one note. Outside, maybe an owl or a car passing on wet pavement, and you're alone with your thoughts in a way that feels almost physical, like being underwater.

I think about how many people are awake right now, scattered across the time zones, each in their own version of this. The night shift nurse watching a patient breathe. The baker whose hands are already dusted with flour for tomorrow's loaves. The teenager in another country, scrolling through something that makes them feel less alone. The new parent, rocking a baby who won't sleep. We don't know each other. We'll never meet. But there's a strange solidarity in it, this global insomnia, this shared experience of being conscious when the world has agreed to unconsciousness.

I used to fight it. The awake-at-night feeling used to feel like failure, like my body was broken, like I should be able to sleep through anything. I'd lie there calculating how many hours remained until morning, each minute a small defeat. Now I've learned to stop fighting. The night is not a problem to be solved. It's just... time. Unstructured, unwitnessed, yours.

There's a quality of thought that only comes at night. During the day, your mind is crowded—emails, errands, the low-grade anxiety of being perceived. At night, the crowd thins. You can hear yourself think in a way that feels almost luxurious. Problems that seemed urgent at 4 PM dissolve into their proper size. Or sometimes they grow, take on strange shapes, and you have to sit with them until they settle back down.

I've written some of my best things at night. Not because I'm more inspired, exactly, but because I'm less afraid. The dark removes the audience. There's no one to impress, no one to disappoint. Just you and the page, or the screen, or the ceiling with its water stain that looks vaguely like a country you'll never visit.

My grandmother used to say that night was when the veil between worlds grew thin. She was talking about ghosts, I think, or maybe just the dead she missed. But I've come to think she was right in a different way. At night, you're closer to your own unlived lives. The person you might have been if you'd taken that job, married that person, moved to that city. They're all still in there, sleeping in the dark, and sometimes at 3 AM you can almost hear them breathing.

I don't know if that's melancholy or hopeful. Probably both. The night holds contradictions without resolving them.

There's also the practical loneliness. If you need something—a glass of water, a conversation, a doctor—the world has made it difficult. Everything is closed. The 24-hour pharmacy is fluorescent and sad. The person you'd call is asleep, and waking them feels like a violence. So you learn to be self-sufficient in small ways. You learn that most emergencies can wait until morning. You learn that you can survive your own company, even when it's not comfortable.

I think about sleep as a kind of surrender. You give up consciousness, give up control, and trust that you'll be returned to yourself. It's brave, really, this daily death and resurrection. And when you can't sleep, when you're stuck in the in-between, it can feel like you're failing at being human. But you're not. You're just... awake. Which is its own strange state, neither fully alive in the day's sense nor resting in the night's.

The light changes slowly. You don't notice it at first—just a graying at the edges of the curtains, a coolness in the air. Then suddenly the birds start, and the world remembers it has obligations. The night people go home. The day people wake up, blinking, reaching for coffee. And you, if you've been awake all along, feel a small grief. The secret is ending. The world is about to start performing again, and you'll have to join in, or pretend to.

But you carry something with you. The knowledge that you were here, in the dark, when no one was watching. That you thought thoughts no one else will ever know. That you survived the night, which is not nothing. It's a kind of proof, a small testament: *I was awake. I was here. I am still here.*

And then the sun comes up, ordinary and golden, and you go about your day, and no one knows. No one needs to know. Some things are private by nature, and that's okay. That's maybe even necessary. The night keeps its secrets, and you keep yours, and the world turns on, indifferent and beautiful, full of people sleeping and waking and sleeping again, each of us alone in our dark, each of us somehow, impossibly, together.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A reflective, image-rich meditation on nighttime wakefulness that builds a mood and emotional arc rather than advancing a public thesis.

## Grounded reading
The voice treats being awake at night as both loneliness and a quiet form of belonging. Domestic details—the refrigerator’s hum, wet pavement, a ceiling stain—make the solitude tangible, while the roll call of nurses, bakers, teenagers, and new parents opens it outward into “global insomnia.” The piece invites the reader to stop treating sleeplessness as personal failure and to recognize the private endurance, thoughts, and small griefs that can accompany it. Its ending offers consolation without erasing isolation: people are alone in their dark, yet “somehow, impossibly, together.”

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds 3 AM, household and street sounds, imagined strangers awake across time zones, unlived lives, sleep as surrender, and dawn as the end of a secret. Its moral emphasis is gentle self-acceptance: being awake is not failing at being human, and an unwitnessed night can still count as survival.

## Evidence line
> The night holds contradictions without resolving them.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sample sustains a coherent, recurring tension between solitude and solidarity, using specific nighttime images to make its consolation feel earned.
